```{r}
nn <- readRDS("../results/nn_task3_comparison.rds")
best <- nn$comparison[which.max(nn$comparison$accuracy), ]
repeat_accuracy <- nn$stability_summary$mean[nn$stability_summary$.metric == "accuracy"]
percent <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
```

### HTML scraping

We compared logistic principal component regression using paragraph text alone with a version that also included headings. Of 2,140 HTML pages, 2,068 contained additional heading words. After text filtering, the exported split contained 1,577 training pages and 395 test pages. Both models used 120 components selected through validation. Adding headings reduced test accuracy from **79.5% to 78.7%** and ROC AUC from 0.863 to 0.847, so headings did not improve predictions in this comparison.

### Bigrams

We tested whether word pairs added information beyond individual words. A second logistic regression combined predictions from the word model with bigram components. Validation selected 40 bigram components, but test accuracy decreased from **79.2% to 78.7%**, and ROC AUC decreased from 0.863 to 0.858. These results did not show a clear benefit from adding bigrams.

### Neural net

We trained small neural networks on TF-IDF text features with early stopping. Ten configurations varied network size, dropout, vocabulary size, word pairs, and the validation share.

The best recorded configuration used 25 hidden units, 0.2 dropout, and an 8,000-term vocabulary of words and word pairs. It achieved **`r percent(best$accuracy)` accuracy** on the same 395 test pages, matching the reported **79.5%** paragraph-only PCR accuracy. Its ROC AUC was `r sprintf("%.3f", best$roc_auc)`, below PCR's 0.863. Four additional runs of a separate bigram configuration averaged `r percent(repeat_accuracy)` accuracy. The results show that a neural network can match the reported accuracy benchmark in one run, but do not establish a consistent improvement over PCR.
